Quaternion Detective

Given 4 numbers, can you find the scalar? (Spoiler: Not always).
Interactive visualization of the W-First vs W-Last convention problem.

lightbulb

Can you identify the scalar without the convention?

Mathematically: No. A quaternion is just an ordered tuple of 4 real numbers. Without context (like "this is a small rotation"), the tuple (0.5, 0.5, 0.5, 0.5) is ambiguous. It produces two completely different rotations depending on whether you interpret the scalar as the first element (w, x, y, z) or the last (x, y, z, w).

Practically: Often, yes. If your data represents an animation or orientation that is near the "identity" (no rotation), the scalar component w will be close to 1.0 or -1.0, while the vector components x, y, z will be close to 0.

Why the "Identity Heuristic" Works

Most animation data stores "small" rotations relative to a base pose. Adjust the angle below to see how the scalar component (W) dominates the vector components (XYZ) when the angle is small.

check_circle Easy to Identify: W is dominant. Most heuristic algorithms would correctly guess the scalar here.
warning Ambiguous: Rotation is large (>90°). W is small or zero. Impossible to distinguish scalar from vector parts numerically.

Common Library Conventions

Unity

Game Engine
x, y, z, w

The standard for most modern game engines. W is stored last.

Unreal Engine

Game Engine
x, y, z, w

Consistent with Unity. Scalar component is at the end.

Eigen

C++ Math Lib
w, x, y, z

Follows the mathematical convention (Hamilton). Scalar first.

GLM (OpenGL)

C++ Math Lib
It's Complicated

Constructor: quat(w,x,y,z)
Memory: x,y,z,w
Access via array index [3] gives w.

Three.js

Web 3D
x, y, z, w (Internal)

Constructor takes x,y,z,w. Iterating the object yields this order.

Blender (Python)

3D Software
w, x, y, z

Uses W-First convention in its Mathutils module.
